basic_info.title: Hidden Markov Map Matching Through Noise and Sparseness

venue.name: 17th ACM SIGSPATIAL International Conference on Advances in Geographic Information Systems (ACM SIGSPATIAL GIS 2009)

basic_info.code_available: no (no official author code; widely re-implemented, e.g. https://github.com/bmwcarit/offline-map-matching and https://github.com/julienperret/mapmatcher)

method.notes: HMM over GPS points: hidden states are candidate road segments near each GPS fix. Emission (measurement) probability is a zero-mean Gaussian on great-circle distance from GPS point to candidate segment; transition probability compares great-circle distance between consecutive GPS points to the road-network route distance between candidate segments (penalizing implausible routes). Most likely road sequence found by the Viterbi algorithm. No learned parameters beyond a couple of hand-tuned constants (GPS noise sigma, transition rate); robust to noisy/sparse and 'junk' points. Output is an ordered sequence of road segments (a route).

gap_analysis.whats_missing: Has none of the three hybrid pillars: no transformer / no neural encoder of a vectorized semantically-enriched graph, no learned latent space and no RL-based sequential decision-making (Viterbi is exact dynamic programming over a fixed probabilistic model), and although it needs no ground-truth labels it learns nothing from data at all (no representation learning, no exploitation of fleet mobility patterns). Uses only raw geometry and shortest-path route distances, with zero road-type/POI/RDF semantics.
gap_analysis.novelty_reasoning: This is the canonical pre-deep-learning baseline; it is essentially orthogonal to the hybrid hypothesis and does not foreshadow a learned, semantic, latent-space RL approach, so the hybrid is genuinely unoccupied relative to this work. Its label-free nature is a hand-built probabilistic model rather than the label-free self-supervised/RL learning the thesis proposes.

relevance.bmw_relevance: Foundational, BMW-relevant baseline: the bmwcarit team maintains an open-source HMM offline-map-matching implementation of exactly this algorithm, making it the natural classical comparator for any learned fleet-trajectory map-matcher in the Foresight project.
